summary: This blog article by Dr. Marco Mancini introduces functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) as a non-invasive optical imaging technique that measures blood oxygenation changes, and explains why it is attractive for neuromarketing compared with fMRI. It covers fNIRS's advantages (movement, portability, low cost, real-time use, temporal resolution), summarizes a 2018 Lee et al. proposal and a follow-up study on prefrontal cortex activation, and lists other applications such as human factors training and clinical rehabilitation.
one_line: Overview of fNIRS, a portable, low-cost optical brain imaging method contrasted with fMRI and applied in neuromarketing research.
key_facts: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is described as a non-invasive optical imaging technique that measures blood oxygenation changes similar to fMRI.
fNIRS measures changes in hemoglobin (Hb) concentrations within the brain by means of the characteristic absorption spectra of Hb in the near-infrared range.
The fMRI experimental setup requires the total immobility of subjects, who must lie down inside the scanner, which is most of the time located inside a hospital.

Companies and academics in neuromarketing and consumer neuroscience usually do not own an fMRI and instead have special agreements with public and private institutes operating in the healthcare industry.
The article lists movement, portability, low cost, real-time assessment of regional oxygenation, and temporal resolution as reasons for the growing interest of neuromarketing experts in fNIRS.
fNIRS temporal resolution is up to 100 Hz, though usually 1–10 Hz, and is not comparable to EEG, which captures neural events in the order of milliseconds.
In 2018, Lee et al. highlighted the advantages of fNIRS in neuromarketing, proposing its integration among the most effective neuromarketing methods.
A follow-up study including two small fNIRS experiments reported significant differences in activation of prefrontal cortex between different tested stimuli.
That study found higher activation when viewing labels and brands compared to non-labeled products.
That study found significantly higher activation when in drinking cola compared to just viewing a picture.

The article states that fNIRS is widely applied beyond neuromarketing for safety simulations and training for airline pilots, train engineers, ship captains, truck drivers, and air traffic controllers.

Other fNIRS applications listed include military simulations and training, in-home real-time monitoring during patient rehabilitation for cognitive impairment or depression, and as a replacement for or supplement to functional brain imaging.
The article states that about 95% of all thought, emotion, and learning occur in the unconscious mind, according to the site's Neuromarketing page teaser.
